processing-001.question: What is the main cause of a "shrinkage cavity," a void that tends to form inside a casting, especially at the center of a thick section that solidifies last?
choices: Gas dissolved in the melt is released during solidification
After solidification, the solid contracts as it cools and cracks because it is restrained by the mold
The volume shrinkage on going from liquid to solid cannot be compensated by melt from the surroundings
processing-001.explanation: Most metals shrink by a few percent in volume on solidification (about 7% for pure aluminum). Solidification proceeds inward from the mold wall, so when a thick section that solidifies last becomes isolated, surrounded by solid, its shrinkage cannot be made up by melt, and a shrinkage cavity with a rough inner surface forms. Countermeasures are to make the riser solidify after the casting so that it can feed melt, and to use chills and similar means so that solidification proceeds progressively toward the riser. Release of dissolved gas produces gas porosity (blowholes) with smooth, round inner surfaces, a different defect. Restrained contraction after solidification produces cracks (hot tears or cold cracks), which differ from a shrinkage cavity, which is a void.

processing-002.question: Which casting method makes a pattern of the same shape as the product from wax, coats it with several layers of refractory slurry and hardens them, then heats it to melt out the wax and pours melt into the resulting mold?
choices: High-pressure die casting
Green-sand casting
Investment casting
processing-002.explanation: In investment casting (the lost-wax process) the pattern is melted out, so the mold does not have to be split to remove it, and complex shapes can be made with good dimensional accuracy and smooth surfaces. The refractory mold withstands high temperatures, so the method is also used for precision parts in Ni-based superalloys, such as jet-engine turbine blades, and directionally solidified and single-crystal blades are made this way as well. Die casting injects melts of aluminum, magnesium and the like into metal dies under high pressure; it is highly productive and suited to thin-walled parts, but not to high-melting steels. Sand casting makes a sand mold from a pattern such as a wooden one and then withdraws the pattern; it can make large parts, but the surface is rough.

processing-003.question: A plate 20 mm thick is cold rolled in several passes to 5.0 mm, assuming the width does not change. Which value is closest to the magnitude of the true strain in the thickness direction, ln(h₀/h)?
processing-003.explanation: The true strain is ln(h₀/h) = ln(20/5.0) = ln 4 ≈ 1.39. 0.75 is the fractional reduction in thickness (20 − 5)/20, and 3.0 is the nominal strain (4 − 1)/1 when the length becomes 4 times at constant volume. True strain has the advantage that intermediate steps can be added together. For example, rolling in two passes, 20 mm → 10 mm → 5 mm, gives a true strain of ln 2 ≈ 0.69 for each pass, and the sum equals the overall 1.39, whereas adding reductions of 50% for each pass does not give the overall 75%. Also, since the volume is constant, the true strain in the length direction is ln 4 ≈ 1.39 as well, equal in magnitude to the thickness strain and opposite in sign.

processing-004.question: When carbon steel parts of the same shape are made by casting and by hot forging, the forged part generally has better toughness and fatigue strength. Which reason is correct?
choices: The cast structure is broken up and refined, small internal voids are pressed shut, and grain flow lines form along the shape
Hot forging suppresses recovery and recrystallization, leaving heavy work hardening that makes the part several times harder than a casting
The large strain of forging stabilizes austenite, so the crystal structure of carbon steel stays FCC all the way down to room temperature
processing-004.explanation: In hot forging, the coarse columnar and dendritic cast structure is broken up by large deformation and recrystallization into fine equiaxed grains. Small internal shrinkage cavities and pores are pressed shut and disappear, as long as they are not connected to the surface. In addition, inclusions and segregation are stretched in the direction of deformation, forming streaky grain flow lines (fiber flow) that follow the shape of the part, and the toughness and fatigue strength along them are higher (across the flow lines they are actually lower, so dies are designed to make the flow follow the shape). In hot working, recovery and recrystallization take place during working, so almost no work hardening remains, and the option citing large residual work hardening is wrong. Nor does forging leave carbon steel as FCC austenite down to room temperature, so the option saying it stays FCC is also wrong.

processing-005.question: An aluminum alloy billet 100 mm in diameter is hot extruded into a round bar 25 mm in diameter. Using the extrusion ratio R = A₀/A (the ratio of cross-sectional areas), take the ideal extrusion pressure, ignoring friction and redundant deformation, as p = Y ln R with a flow stress Y = 50 MPa. Which value is closest to p?
choices: About 69 MPa
About 139 MPa
About 800 MPa
processing-005.explanation: Cross-sectional area is proportional to the square of the diameter, so the extrusion ratio is R = (100/25)² = 16. Then p = Y ln R = 50 × ln 16 ≈ 50 × 2.77 ≈ 139 MPa. About 69 MPa takes the logarithm of the diameter ratio of 4, and about 800 MPa uses Y × R without the logarithm. The actual extrusion pressure is considerably higher than this ideal value because of friction with the container wall and die and the redundant shear deformation inside the material. Indirect extrusion, in which the die moves and there is no sliding between billet and container, requires less pressure than direct extrusion, in which the billet slides through the container.

processing-006.question: Ignoring changes in thickness and the radius at the bottom corner, a cylindrical cup with a bottom, 50 mm in diameter and 40 mm high, is made from a circular blank in a single deep-drawing operation. Assuming the surface area does not change, which value is closest to the diameter of the blank?
choices: About 81 mm
About 102 mm
About 130 mm
processing-006.explanation: The surface area of the cup is the sum of the bottom area πd²/4 and the side area πdh. Setting this equal to the blank area πD²/4 gives D² = d² + 4dh = 50² + 4 × 50 × 40 = 2500 + 8000 = 10500, so D ≈ 102 mm. About 130 mm is d + 2h, obtained by simply folding the side wall outward flat, which ignores the circumferential contraction of the outer part of the blank as it is drawn in; about 81 mm, √(d² + 2dh), halves the side area by taking it as πrh (r being the radius) instead of 2πrh. The ratio of blank diameter to cup diameter (the drawing ratio) is about 2.05, and since the limiting drawing ratio of steel sheet is roughly 2 to 2.2 (depending on the r-value and other factors), a single draw is close to the limit, and in practice the work is sometimes split with redrawing.

processing-007.question: When a sheet is bent and removed from the die, its bend angle partly recovers by elastic recovery (springback). Which is likely to show larger springback? Assume the same sheet thickness and bend radius.
choices: A soft, stiff material with a low yield stress and a high Young's modulus
It is set only by the working speed, regardless of yield stress or Young's modulus
A material with a high yield stress and a low Young's modulus
processing-007.explanation: Even after plastic deformation, stresses of about the yield stress remain across the section of a bent sheet, and when the load is removed it springs back by the corresponding elastic strain (roughly σ/E). Springback is therefore larger the higher the yield stress and the lower the Young's modulus. High-strength steel sheet, with the same Young's modulus but higher strength, and aluminum alloy sheet, with a Young's modulus about one-third that of steel, show large springback and are harder to bring to shape. The option of a soft and stiff material is the reverse, and the option saying it is set only by the working speed is also wrong. Countermeasures include overbending by the amount of recovery and pressing the bend firmly in the die so that the bend region deforms plastically.

processing-008.question: The carbon equivalent used as a guide to the weldability of steel is Ceq = C + Mn/6 + (Cr + Mo + V)/5 + (Ni + Cu)/15 (mass %). Which value is closest to Ceq for a steel with 0.20% C, 1.20% Mn, 0.30% Cr, 0.10% Mo, 0% V, 0.30% Ni and 0.15% Cu?
choices: About 0.40%
About 0.51%
About 2.25%
processing-008.explanation: Calculating each term gives C = 0.20, Mn/6 = 0.20, (Cr + Mo + V)/5 = 0.40/5 = 0.08 and (Ni + Cu)/15 = 0.45/15 = 0.03, for a total of Ceq = 0.51%. About 0.40% stops after the C and Mn terms, and about 2.25% simply adds up the element contents without dividing by the coefficients. The carbon equivalent converts the effect of each alloying element on hardenability into an amount of carbon and sums them. The higher the Ceq of a steel, the more readily the weld heat-affected zone is quenched into hard martensite and the greater the risk of cold cracking. As a guide, steels with Ceq up to about 0.4% can often be welded without preheating, while above that, preheating becomes necessary depending on plate thickness, restraint and hydrogen content.

processing-009.question: Arc welding is carried out at a voltage of 25 V, a current of 200 A and a welding speed of 300 mm/min. With an arc thermal efficiency of 0.80, which value is closest to the heat input per mm of weld, Q = ηVI/v?
choices: About 13 J/mm
About 0.80 kJ/mm
About 1.0 kJ/mm
processing-009.explanation: Converting the welding speed to per second gives v = 300/60 = 5.0 mm/s. The arc power is VI = 25 × 200 = 5000 W, so Q = 0.80 × 5000/5.0 = 800 J/mm = 0.80 kJ/mm. About 1.0 kJ/mm forgets to multiply by the thermal efficiency, and about 13 J/mm divides by the per-minute value of 300 as is. A larger heat input slows the cooling of the weld, making the heat-affected zone less likely to harden, but it lengthens the time at high temperature, so grains can coarsen and toughness can fall. Upper and lower limits on heat input are therefore set according to the type of steel to control the cooling rate.

processing-010.question: In welding high-strength steel, preheating is used to prevent cold cracking (hydrogen cracking), which appears in the heat-affected zone and elsewhere within minutes to days after welding. Which statement correctly describes the effect of preheating?
choices: It slows the cooling of the weld so that hard martensite is less likely to form, and gives diffusible hydrogen time to escape
It speeds solidification of the weld metal, preventing hot cracking from impurities gathering at the end of solidification
It quenches the weld rapidly, hardening it to make it resistant to cracking
processing-010.explanation: Cold cracking occurs when three things coincide: diffusible hydrogen that has entered the weld metal, a hard, low-toughness microstructure (martensite), and tensile stress from restraint of the weld. Preheating lengthens the cooling time through the range of 800 to 500°C, suppressing hardening, and also lengthens the time held at high temperature, making it easier for hydrogen to diffuse out. Using low-hydrogen electrodes after drying them and postheating right after welding are countermeasures with the same purpose. Hot cracking (solidification cracking) is the tearing of liquid films enriched in segregated elements such as P and S at the final stage of solidification, and both its mechanism and its countermeasures differ. Rapid quenching to harden the weld actually makes cold cracking more likely.

processing-011.question: When austenitic stainless steels such as SUS304 are welded, intergranular corrosion can occur in the heat-affected zone a short distance from the weld line (weld decay). Which combination of cause and countermeasure is correct?
choices: The heat of welding turns austenite in the heat-affected zone into martensite, weakening the grain boundaries. Quench again after welding
The high temperature in the fusion zone evaporates Cr, dropping the weld metal's Cr content below 12%. Use a Cr-rich electrode and increase the welding heat input
In zones heated to about 500 to 800°C, Cr carbides precipitate at grain boundaries, leaving Cr-depleted zones. Use SUS304L or Ti- or Nb-added steels
processing-011.explanation: In the heat-affected zone a short distance from the weld line, there is a band exposed for some time to temperatures of about 500 to 800°C. There, Cr carbides such as Cr₂₃C₆ precipitate at grain boundaries, and the Cr concentration right next to the boundaries falls to a level that cannot sustain passivity, so corrosion proceeds along the grain boundaries. This is called sensitization. Countermeasures are to use a low-carbon steel (SUS304L) with less of the carbon that forms the carbides, to use stabilized steels (SUS321 or SUS347) in which carbon is tied up as Ti or Nb carbides, and to give a solution heat treatment after welding to dissolve the carbides again. Austenitic stainless steels do not become martensite on quenching, and Cr evaporation is not the main cause either.

processing-012.question: Which statement correctly describes the features of friction stir welding (FSW)?
choices: A rotating tool's frictional heat softens the material below its melting point to stir and join it, so pores and solidification cracks are rare
It is a type of arc welding in which the joint is heated above its melting point and filler metal is added while a rotating tool stirs the molten weld pool
A high-energy electron beam melts the material locally and penetrates deeply into it, so the joining can only be done inside a large vacuum chamber
processing-012.explanation: In friction stir welding, a tool with a protrusion (probe) at its tip is rotated and plunged into the abutting joint, the material softened by frictional heat is made to flow plastically and mix, and the tool then travels along the joint line. Because it is solid-state joining in which the material does not melt, the porosity and solidification cracking that are problems in fusion welding do not occur, and the joint consists of fine recrystallized grains. It can join 2000- and 7000-series aluminum alloys, which are prone to hot cracking in fusion welding, and it is used for railway car and ship members. The descriptions of arc welding, which heats above the melting point, and of electron beam welding belong to other joining methods. Using it on high-melting steels or titanium requires tool materials that resist wear at high temperature.

processing-013.question: A green compact at 70% relative density is sintered to 95% relative density. Assuming isotropic shrinkage and no change in mass, which value is closest to the linear shrinkage (fractional decrease in length) due to sintering?
choices: About 9.7%
About 26%
About 36%
processing-013.explanation: Since the mass does not change, the volume is inversely proportional to the density, so V/V₀ = 0.70/0.95 ≈ 0.737. Because the shrinkage is isotropic, the length ratio is the cube root of the volume ratio, (0.737)^(1/3) ≈ 0.903, and the linear shrinkage is 1 − 0.903 ≈ 9.7%. About 26% is the volume shrinkage 1 − 0.737, and about 36% is the increase in relative density (0.95 − 0.70)/0.70; neither is the fractional decrease in length. When making sintered parts, the die dimensions are made larger to allow for this shrinkage. If the green density varies from place to place, because of friction with the die wall and the like, the shrinkage also varies, causing warping and dimensional scatter after sintering.

processing-014.question: To make WC–Co cemented carbide, WC powder is mixed with Co powder, compacted and sintered. Which statement correctly describes this sintering?
choices: A Co-rich liquid wets the WC grains, and rearrangement and solution–reprecipitation give almost full density (liquid-phase sintering)
Below the melting point of Co (about 1495°C) no liquid forms, and the Co evaporates during sintering, leaving a porous body of WC alone
The whole body is heated above the melting point of WC to melt it, then solidified in a mold as in casting to make it dense
processing-014.explanation: In the WC–Co system, a eutectic reaction between WC and Co produces a liquid phase at a temperature below the melting point of Co (about 1495°C). At the sintering temperature the Co-rich liquid wets the WC particles well, capillary forces rearrange and pack the particles, and small WC particles dissolve and reprecipitate onto larger ones, so the body densifies to nearly full density. This is liquid-phase sintering. After cooling, Co remains as the binder phase that holds the hard WC particles together and provides toughness. WC has an extremely high melting point, and melting and casting it is not practical, so it is made by powder metallurgy. Co is not lost by evaporation during sintering; it is indispensable as the binder phase.

processing-015.question: Hot isostatic pressing (HIP) is used to eliminate closed pores remaining inside powder-metallurgy parts and castings. Which describes the method correctly?
choices: At room temperature, powder in a rubber mold is compacted by applying pressure isotropically through a liquid
At high temperature, the powder is sintered under uniaxial pressure from upper and lower punches while current is passed
At high temperature, an inert gas such as argon is used as the pressure medium to apply an equally high pressure from all directions
processing-015.explanation: In HIP the part is placed in a pressure vessel and, while heated to high temperature, an equal pressure of about 100 MPa or more is applied from all directions by an inert gas such as argon. Closed internal pores collapse and disappear by creep and diffusion, raising density and fatigue strength without greatly changing the shape. It is also used to eliminate pores in turbine-blade castings and in metal parts made by additive manufacturing. Open pores connected to the surface do not collapse because gas enters them, so the part is first sintered until the pores close, or the powder is sealed in a metal container (capsule) for treatment. Using a rubber mold at room temperature is cold isostatic pressing (CIP), and pressing in one direction while passing current is a method such as spark plasma sintering.
